newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BOSKALIS SEES BIG WORLD DREDGING GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: BOSKALIS SEES BIG WORLD DREDGING GROWTH.

text.p: Dutch dredger Boskalis said on Thursday the outlook for the world dredging market in the coming years was very healthy with little risk of overcapacity as major new projects came on stream.

"In our vision there is no danger of structural overcapacity in the next few years because there is too much work coming onto the market," Boskalis chairman Rob van Gelder told a results news conference.
The added "jumbo hopper" capacity now being built by European opertors would be utilized by a series of large-scale projects, particularly in the Far East, he said.
"Market conditions in the Far East picked up in the second 1996 half, and this will continue," Van Gelder said.

In Singapore the land reclamation programme was progressing steadily, while contracts for Hong Kong's container terminal 9 were expected to be awarded this year and the market in Malaysia was also picking up, he said.

Board member Leo Vellekamp said contracts worth some 1.5 billion guilders for the first phase of the Singapore land reclamation project had already been awarded, but that the second phase was thought to be worth much more.
Some 60 to 70 percent of the second phase would involve dredging work, he said.

Van Gelder said Boskalis' investment in the jumbo 23,425 cubic metre trailing suction hopper dredger WD Fairway, due to be taken into use this year, was aimed at meeting the global trend towards large-scale offshore land reclamation projects.
The Fairway and its sister vessel, due to be delivered in summer 1998, will require investments of some 150 million guilders in 1997 and 60 million in 1998, he said.
"In the next ten years there will be more dredging work than there has been for a long time," Van Gelder said.
But he added: "I will not say that there is no reason to expect there will be no periods of weakness in the longer term."
Price competition would likely continue and Boskalis would have to fight to maintain steady profit growth, he said.
